[DAY-24] A story that takes place 100 years in the future.

"Dear Passengers. You may now unfasten your seat belts and use the restrooms. As per standard safety procedures, please do not launch off the wall or throw any kind of object. Always keep one hand holding onto a secured object and ask our micro-gravity attendants for any assistance. Enjoy your space flight, and thank you for choosing Firefly Space Transit."

John gave an accustomed sigh as he unlatched the four, or five, buckles that secured him since launch off. This wasn't his first trip to the moon. He had a job at the moon and frequently came back down to Earth to see his wife and child. Ava would soon be 18, eligible to ride a space shuttle. She was excited for her first trip to space.

John could barely remember how it felt to lose feeling in your leg or to feel the pressure on your entire body for the first time. How frightening and exhilarating it was to experience something the brain had no precedence for, when space travel wasn't old enough yet to be considered a conquered territory. The magic of it all seems to fade to nostalgia. The excitement went away with routine.

The window next to him was closed during the launch off. Although it was designed to filter anything that could harm him permanently, the intense burning during launch off bothered his eyes. His younger self would have never closed the blinds. Now, he opened them. He saw the planet atmosphere and its green tinge off the earthly horizon, giving way to the black, lightless emptiness dotted with stars millions or billions of years younger than what it actually is, mixed with the quick glints of satellites.

It was a sight no longer unfamiliar. But something felt different. He nudged the stranger next to him.

"What?" Came the slightly annoyed reply.

"I - uh", John stuttered slightly. "My grandparents once told me that a little more than 200 years ago, two brothers learned how to fly off the ground. The plane only stayed up for less than an hour and didn't event go up a kilometer in altitude. A hundred years ago, whenever my grandfather crossed the Atlantic, he wondered what they would have thought of looking down at a floor of clouds...."

"That's nice."

The stranger turned away and John's heart beat a little faster, wondering why he even bothered his fellow passenger. There was a yearning inside him. He wondered if he simply wanted to ward the banality of it all.

But as John looked out at the window, he realized he didn't have to. It was wondrous in and of itself. He simply had to never convince himself it wasn't special.

When he thought of the people he could share this epiphany with, he could only think of Ava. Only one out of hundreds he have known.

It was sad, but the thought also made him happy.
